Gas.definition: The unit that prices EVM computation: every opcode costs gas, and a transaction pays gas used multiplied by the gas price.
Gas.whyItMatters: It is the mechanism that makes a Turing-complete shared machine safe, and it is the single most calculable exam question in this course.
confusions: Gas is not ether: gas is a count of work, gas price is what that work costs.
The gas limit is a ceiling, not a charge - unused gas is refunded.
Running out of gas reverts state but the fee is still spent.

Event.definition: A named record a contract emits that is written to the transaction log rather than to storage.
Event.whyItMatters: It is how an off-chain interface learns that something happened without polling every block.
confusions: An event is not state: a contract cannot read its own past events.
Indexed parameters become searchable topics; a normal event allows up to three.
Events are cheap precisely because they are not in the state trie.

Modifier.definition: A reusable guard declared with the modifier keyword that runs before or after a function body and can reject the call.
Modifier.whyItMatters: It puts authorisation in one place instead of repeating require checks at every function.
confusions: A modifier is not an event and not a function; it wraps a function.

Reentrancy.definition: A vulnerability where an external call is made before the contract updates its own state, letting the callee call back in and act on the stale state.
Reentrancy.whyItMatters: It caused the DAO loss in 2016 and remains the most examined bug in this unit.
confusions: The fix is ordering: update state before the external call (checks-effects-interactions).
A nonReentrant mutex is a second fix, not the only one.

EOA.definition: An externally owned account controlled by a private key, holding no code, that can sign and originate transactions.
EOA.whyItMatters: Only an EOA can start a transaction, so everything on the chain is ultimately reached through one.
confusions: Same address format as a contract account, completely different powers.
An EOA has a nonce that increments with each transaction it sends.

Contract account.definition: An account created by a deployment transaction that holds bytecode and storage and has no private key.
Contract account.whyItMatters: It can hold and move value but can never act first; it only responds to a call.
confusions: It cannot initiate a transaction, on a timer or otherwise.
It can send ether, but only as the effect of a function call it received.

topics.name: Structure of a Contract
topics.definition: A Solidity contract is a class whose instance lives permanently at one address, holding state variables, exposing functions, guarded by modifiers, and announcing changes through events.
topics.problem: A contract must be inspectable and auditable before it is deployed, because after deployment its code cannot be quietly changed. That requires a fixed, small set of structural elements with declared visibility and mutability.
mechanism: Pragma: the compiler version, e.g. pragma solidity ^0.8.20; it selects the language rules.
State variables: the persistent memory, e.g. mapping(address => uint256) public balanceOf; they live in storage and cost gas to write.
Constructor: runs once at deployment, typically to set owner = msg.sender.
Modifiers: reusable guards such as onlyOwner that run before the function body and can revert the call.
Functions: the doors; each declares visibility (public, external, internal, private) and mutability (view, pure, payable).
Events: declared with the event keyword and emitted with emit; they announce state changes to off-chain listeners.
terminology: Persistent storage slot owned by the contract.
Who may call: public, external, internal, private.
Whether the function reads, writes, or accepts value.

examAnswer.question: Annotate a Solidity contract: name each structural element and state its role.
points: pragma: fixes the compiler version and therefore the language rules.
State variables: persistent memory; declare visibility on them too.
constructor: sets initial state once, at deployment; msg.sender is the deployer.
Functions: the callable interface; declare visibility and mutability on each.
Modifiers: reusable authorisation checks that run before the body.
Events: off-chain announcements, cheap because they are logs not storage.

traps: Visibility is not access control in the security sense - private is not secret on-chain, it only restricts Solidity-level calls.
A function marked view cannot write state; marking it payable is what allows it to receive ether.
Constructors run once; anything you need at call time belongs in a function or modifier.
topics.revision: pragma -> state variables -> constructor -> functions (+ visibility/mutability) -> modifiers -> events.
recall: What does the pragma line control?
The compiler version, and therefore the language rules in force.
Where does msg.sender point inside a constructor?
The deploying account (an EOA or a factory contract).
What is the difference between view and payable?
view promises no state write; payable allows the function to receive ether.
Why are events cheaper than state writes?
They are written to the log, outside the state trie.

topics.name: Setting up and Interacting with a Contract using Geth Client
topics.definition: Deploying a contract from geth means sending a transaction whose data field is the compiled bytecode and which has no recipient; the contract address is then derived from the sender and its nonce.
topics.problem: You need a way to put code on a chain without any privileged deployment API. Since the chain only understands transactions, deployment must be expressible as one.
mechanism: geth init --datadir ./node: creates the chain database and keystore.
Start the node: geth --datadir ./node --networkid 1 --http --port 8545 exposes JSON-RPC on 8545.
Create an account: personal.newAccount() prints an address; personal.unlockAccount(acct, "", 0) unlocks it for signing.
Deploy: eth.sendTransaction({from: acct, data: bytecode}) with no to field - the receipt's contractAddress is the new address.
Call: eth.sendTransaction({from: acct, to: contractAddress, data: selector + encoded args}).
Read: eth.call({to: addr, data: selector}) executes without changing state and costs no gas.
terminology: The HTTP/WebSocket API a client exposes.
The record returned once a transaction is mined; contains contractAddress and logs.
The first 4 bytes of keccak256 of the function signature.
The folder holding chain and keys.

examAnswer.question: Give the command sequence to deploy and then call a contract from geth.
points: geth init --datadir ./node creates the chain and keystore.
geth --datadir ./node --networkid 1 --http --port 8545 starts a node and exposes RPC.
personal.newAccount() then personal.unlockAccount(acct, "", 0) creates and unlocks a signing key.
Deploy with eth.sendTransaction({from, data: bytecode}) and no recipient.
Read the address from the transaction receipt's contractAddress.
Call with eth.sendTransaction({from, to: addr, data: selector}) or read free with eth.call.

traps: Deployment has no 'to' field - if you set one, you are calling, not deploying.
eth.call is read-only and free; eth.sendTransaction is a state change and costs gas.
geth holds the chain; it is not a wallet - keys are unlocked locally, signing is still done by the key.
topics.revision: init -> run node -> new + unlock account -> send tx with data=bytecode (no to) -> read contractAddress from receipt -> call with to + selector.
recall: Where does the new contract's address appear?
In the deployment transaction's receipt, as contractAddress.
How do you distinguish deploy from call in the transaction?
Deploy has no to field; call sets to the contract address.
What does geth attach do?
Opens an interactive JavaScript console against a running node.
Which call costs no gas?
eth.call - it executes without changing state.

topics.name: Gas
topics.definition: Gas is the unit that prices EVM computation: every opcode has a fixed cost, the machine meters what your code spends, and the transaction is charged gas used multiplied by the gas price.
topics.problem: The EVM is a shared, replicated machine. Without a price on computation, one contract with an infinite loop would stall every node on the network forever.
mechanism: The transaction declares a gas limit - the maximum it may spend.
Each opcode executed adds its fixed cost to the running meter (gas used).
If gas used reaches the limit, execution halts, state is reverted, and the fee is still spent.
If it completes, unused gas is refunded and the charge is gas used x gas price.
Opcode prices encode policy: storage writes are expensive, reads and pure computation are cheap, so contracts are nudged to keep little state.
Under EIP-1559 the fee is a burned base fee plus a priority tip paid to the validator.
terminology: Price per gas unit, in gwei.

examAnswer.question: What is gas and why does Ethereum charge it?
points: Gas meters computational work, so resources are priced rather than free.
It bounds execution: an infinite loop runs out of gas and is reverted, which is what makes a Turing-complete chain safe.
Fee = gas used x gas price; the limit is a ceiling and unused gas is refunded.
Opcode prices encode policy - storage costly, computation cheap.
Running out of gas reverts state but not the fee, so it is never a free retry.
Post-1559 the fee splits into a burned base fee and a validator tip.

traps: Gas is not the fee. Gas is work; the fee is gas x price.
Unused gas is refunded; the limit is not what you pay.
An out-of-gas revert still costs the sender - it is not a cancelled transaction.
topics.revision: Fee = gas used x gas price. 1 ETH = 1e9 gwei. 40,000 gas at 25 gwei = 1,000,000 gwei = 0.001 ETH.
recall: Compute the fee for 40,000 gas at 25 gwei.
What happens to unused gas?
It is refunded; only gas used is charged.
Why does gas exist at all?
To bound execution so an infinite loop cannot stall the chain.
Which is dearer: a storage write or a pure computation?
A storage write, deliberately - to discourage bloated state.

topics.name: Logs
topics.definition: Logs are records written into the transaction receipt rather than into contract storage, so they are cheap to emit but cannot be read back by the contract.
topics.problem: If every announcement had to be a storage write, telling the world what happened would cost as much as changing state. Most announcements are for outside observers, not for future contract logic.
mechanism: When a contract emits an event, the node writes a log entry into the receipt.
The log lives outside the state trie, so it does not change the state root and costs far less than a storage write.
Because it is outside storage, Solidity code has no instruction to read a past log.
Outside code reads logs through receipts or the log filter (eth_getLogs), which is what block explorers do.
That makes logs a one-way channel: excellent for telling the world, useless for logic that must consult history.
terminology: A receipt entry produced by emit.
The mined transaction's result record, containing logs and gas used.
The RPC method that filters logs by address and topic.
Where storage lives; logs are deliberately outside it.

examAnswer.question: Distinguish logs from state variables, and explain the consequence for contracts.
points: Storage is part of the state trie; logs live in the receipt.
Storage is readable by the contract; logs are invisible to it.
Storage writes are costly and change the state root; logs are cheap and do not.
Consequence: a contract cannot make logic depend on its own past logs.
Off-chain readers use receipts and log filters to react to events.
Design rule: emit for observers, store for logic.

traps: Do not claim a contract can read its own events - it cannot.
Logs do not change state, so they cannot be used as a counter the contract reads.
Cheap does not mean free: emitting still costs gas, just far less than storage.
topics.revision: Storage: in the state trie, readable by the contract, costly. Logs: in the receipt, invisible to the contract, cheap.
recall: Why is a log cheaper than a storage write?
It is written to the receipt, outside the state trie, so it does not change the state root.
Can a contract read its own past logs?
No - logs are outside storage and invisible to Solidity code.
What reads logs then?
Off-chain clients, via receipts or eth_getLogs.
What does a log cost in terms of state?
Nothing - it does not alter the state root.

topics.name: Events
topics.definition: An event is a named record a contract declares and emits to announce something, whose indexed parameters become searchable topics that clients can filter on.
topics.problem: A user interface must learn that a transaction happened without downloading and re-executing every block. It needs a cheap, addressable, filterable announcement.
mechanism: Declare the shape: event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value);
Emit it with the payload: emit Transfer(msg.sender, to, amount);
The node writes a log whose first topic is keccak256 of the event signature.
Each indexed parameter becomes an additional topic, so up to three parameters can be searched directly.
A client filters with eth_getLogs by contract address and topics, so it can find every Transfer in history for one address.
The client then reacts: it updates the interface without polling state.
terminology: The statement that writes the log.
Marks a parameter as a searchable topic.
A 32-byte log field; the first is the event signature hash.
An event with no name, filterable only by address.

examAnswer.question: Write an event declaration and its emit, and explain why events are not state.
points: Declaration: event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value);
Emit: emit Transfer(msg.sender, to, amount);
The log's first topic is keccak256 of the signature, so the type is identifiable.
Indexed parameters become topics, so history is filterable by address.
Events are logs, not storage: they cost little and do not change the state root.
A contract cannot read them back, so they serve observers, not logic.

traps: An event is a log, not a state variable - never say events are stored in the contract.
Only indexed parameters are searchable; a fourth indexed parameter is not allowed on a normal event.
Emitting does not change state, so an event cannot be used as a counter.
topics.revision: event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value); emit Transfer(a, b, n). Topic 1 = signature hash; indexed params = filterable.
recall: What is the first topic of an event log?
keccak256 of the event signature, which identifies the type.
How many indexed parameters does an ordinary event allow?
Up to three.
Why is an interface built on events rather than state polling?
Events are cheap, indexed and filterable, so the client learns of changes without re-reading every account.
Can the emitting contract read the event later?
No - it is a log, outside storage.

topics.name: Setting up and Interacting with a Contract using Mist Wallet
topics.definition: Mist was a desktop browser and wallet bundled with a light Ethereum node, letting a user call contracts without pointing at someone else's server; it is discontinued.
topics.problem: Early users needed a way to interact with contracts without running a full node or trusting a third-party RPC endpoint. Mist bundled a light node with the interface.
mechanism: Mist shipped a browser plus a light Ethereum node in one desktop application.
Contracts were called through a normal web interface, but the node behind it was local.
It is discontinued, so only its historical role is examinable.
Its successor pattern is the browser extension wallet plus a remote RPC, which is what MetaMask does.
terminology: A node that verifies headers but not all state.
A wallet shipped inside the browser application.

examAnswer.question: What was Mist, and why is it only historically relevant?
points: A desktop application combining a browser, a wallet and a light Ethereum node.
It let a user call contracts without configuring a separate node or trusting a public RPC.
It is discontinued, so examinable only as ecosystem history.
Its idea survives in the extension-wallet-plus-RPC pattern (MetaMask).

traps: Do not describe Mist as a current tool - the paper may ask for recognition only.
Do not confuse Mist with MetaMask: Mist bundled a node, MetaMask does not.
topics.revision: Mist = browser + wallet + light node, discontinued. Its idea survives as MetaMask + RPC.
recall: What did Mist bundle that MetaMask does not?
A light Ethereum node inside the desktop application.
Is Mist current?
No - it is discontinued and only its historical role is examinable.

topics.name: Smart Contract Examples
topics.definition: A token contract is a ledger of per-address balances with a supply rule; a voting contract records hidden commitments until a deadline and then reveals and counts them. Both are expressible as explicit state transitions.
topics.problem: An examiner wants to see that you can read a contract as a set of legal state transitions rather than as code. The examples exist to make that translation concrete.
mechanism: Token state: balances[address] and totalSupply.
transfer(to, n): require balances[msg.sender] >= n; balances[msg.sender] -= n; balances[to] += n; emit Transfer.
mint(n): restricted to the owner; totalSupply += n; the minter's balance rises.
burn(n): totalSupply -= n; the holder's balance falls.
Voting: commit(choice, salt) stores keccak256(choice, salt, sender) before the deadline, so the choice is hidden.
After the deadline, reveal(choice, salt) is checked against the commitment and counted.
terminology: A legal (input, old state) -> new state mapping.
The sum of all balances; mint and burn are the only ways it moves.
Hide a value by publishing its hash, then reveal it later.
The standard token interface: transfer, approve, balanceOf, totalSupply.

examAnswer.question: Trace a token contract's state transitions and explain the voting variant.
points: State: balances per address plus totalSupply.
transfer moves balance between addresses and leaves totalSupply unchanged.
mint is owner-only and raises totalSupply, diluting every holder's share.
burn lowers totalSupply and the holder's balance.
Every transition emits an event for off-chain tracking.
Voting hides choices with commit-reveal so the outcome cannot be read early.

traps: transfer does not change totalSupply - only mint and burn do.
A voting contract's secrecy comes from hashing, not from access control.
Do not call a token contract 'a database' without saying what the state transitions are.
topics.revision: transfer: A-n, B+n, supply unchanged. mint: supply +n, owner only. burn: supply -n. Voting: commit hash, reveal after deadline.
recall: Which functions change totalSupply?
Only mint and burn; transfer leaves it unchanged.
What does a transfer of 40 from A to B do to supply?
Nothing - balances move, totalSupply stays constant.
How does a voting contract hide choices?
It stores keccak256(choice, salt, sender) and reveals after the deadline.
Who may mint?
The owner, enforced by a modifier.

topics.name: Smart Contract Patterns
topics.definition: Patterns are the standard structural answers to recurring contract mistakes; each one reorders or guards the code so a specific attack stops working.
topics.problem: The same handful of bugs recur because contracts hand control to code they do not control. A pattern is cheaper than re-deriving the fix under exam pressure.
mechanism: Checks-effects-interactions: check the condition, update your state, then make the external call - so a re-entrant call sees the new state.
Pull payment: credit a balance and let the recipient withdraw, instead of pushing funds during the call, so a malicious recipient cannot block or drain.
Owner-only modifier: replace scattered comparisons with one guard, so authorisation lives in one place.
Guard against tx.origin: check msg.sender, because tx.origin can be a phishing intermediary.
State machine: declare an enum of states and allow only legal transitions, so an attacker cannot skip a step.
Checked arithmetic: Solidity 0.8+ reverts on overflow; SafeMath was the pre-0.8 equivalent.
terminology: Calling back into a contract before it finished its state update.
Pay by crediting a balance the recipient withdraws.
A lock flag that rejects re-entry.

examAnswer.question: Name three smart-contract patterns and the failure each one removes.
points: Checks-effects-interactions removes reentrancy by updating state before the external call.
Pull payment removes both reentrancy and the DoS of a recipient that reverts.
Owner-only modifier removes unauthorised calls by centralising the check.
msg.sender over tx.origin removes phishing through an intermediary contract.
State machine removes illegal transitions by construction.
Checked arithmetic removes overflow and underflow.

traps: A pattern is justified by the attack it stops - always name the attack.
checks-effects-interactions is about order, not about adding require statements.
Pull payment is not just 'withdraw later': it is what stops a malicious recipient blocking the send.
topics.revision: CEI -> reentrancy. Pull payment -> reentrancy + DoS. Owner modifier -> unauthorised. msg.sender -> phishing. State machine -> illegal transitions. 0.8 math -> overflow.
recall: What ordering does checks-effects-interactions require?
Check, then update your own state, then call out.
Which pattern replaces repeated require(msg.sender == owner)?
An owner-only modifier.
Why prefer msg.sender over tx.origin?
tx.origin is the original EOA and can be a phishing contract; msg.sender is the immediate caller.
What does pull payment prevent?
A malicious recipient blocking the payment, and reentrancy in the payout path.
